Northern Viking 26 forms part of NATO's broader Arctic Sentry activity, supporting the defence of Iceland and the protection of critical national and NATO infrastructure in the High North. Standing NATO Mine Countermeasures Group One (SNMCMG1), currently under Lithuanian command, is contributing to the exercise alongside Allied maritime and joint forces. Its participation highlights the important role of mine countermeasures (MCM) in maintaining freedom of movement and safeguarding critical maritime routes. The group brings together a multinational MCM capability, with minehunters from Canada, Germany, Lithuania and Poland, supported by a Danish Mine Countermeasures team and a Portuguese Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) team. Together, these forces provide a diverse range of specialist capabilities while strengthening Allied interoperability and readiness in the challenging waters of the North Atlantic. Standing NATO Maritime Group One (SNMG1) also joins the exercise, bringing together NATO's standing maritime forces in the High North. Operating alongside Allied navies, the two task groups will strengthen interoperability across surface, subsurface and mine countermeasure operations, reinforcing NATO's readiness and its ability to safeguard security in the North Atlantic through integrated multinational training. Bringing together the United States and Iceland with NATO Allied forces from Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Lithuania, Germany, Norway and Poland, the exercise integrates air and maritime capabilities in a realistic operational scenario to strengthen interoperability, enhance readiness, and improve the ability to plan and conduct joint multinational operations. For Standing NATO Mine Countermeasures Group One (SNMCMG1), participation provides an opportunity to employ and further develop MCM capabilities in the demanding maritime environment of the North Atlantic and High North. "Exercises such as Northern Viking demonstrate the value of bringing together Allied mine countermeasures forces with other maritime and joint capabilities. By training together in a demanding operational environment, we strengthen interoperability, share operational experience and improve our readiness to contribute to the security of the North Atlantic," said Commander SNMCMG1, Lithuanian Navy Commander Donatas Gečas. The exercise also underlines the strategic importance of the North Atlantic and the Greenland-Iceland-United Kingdom (GIUK) Gap. The waters between Greenland and Iceland, and between Iceland and the United Kingdom, form a critical maritime corridor connecting North America and Europe. Operating in this challenging environment allows Allied forces to build familiarity with the unique conditions of the region while strengthening their ability to operate together in support of NATO's collective defence. SNMG1 and SNMCMG1 are two of NATO's four Standing Naval Forces, maintained at high readiness to provide persistent maritime security, assure freedom of navigation and respond rapidly to emerging threats across the Alliance. Photograph: Naina Helen Jama/EPA Sweden Sweden must apologise for harm done to Sami people, says state-backed report Independent commission accuses country of failing Indigenous people, amid rising tensions over land rights Miranda Bryant Nordic correspondent Wed 30 Sep 2026 11.40 EDT Last modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 12.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An independent commission set up by the Swedish state has called on the country’s government to apologise for the “harm and injustice inflicted upon the Sami people” and to start a national process for “redress and reconciliation”. The Truth Commission for the Sami People also called for a special apology to be issued urgently to elderly Sami people who were forced as children to attend segregated so-called “nomad school” and other boarding schools where they were “subjected to violations or abuse”. ‘The same struggles as 100 years ago’: exhibition highlights lives of Sami people in Sweden Read more The commission’s report, published on Wednesday, is the outcome of a four-year investigation and hundreds of interviews with Sami people across Sweden. It was due to be presented to a government representative at a ceremony featuring readings from the text, but with no government yet in place after the election earlier this month , it went instead to Parisa Liljestrand, the last government’s culture minister. The commission’s chair, Lena Nyberg, told her: “We hand over a big responsibility.” Liljestrand thanked the members of the commission and those who were interviewed for the report, saying it had been a “historic process”. There have been similar truth commissions into the treatment of Sami people – Europe’s only recognised Indigenous people – in Norway and Finland. Norway has issued an official apology and discussions in Finland are ongoing. The new report accuses Sweden of failing to meet its domestic and international human rights obligations and says that as a “direct consequence” of mistreatment, the Sami people today face “major challenges” in preserving and developing their culture. View image in fullscreen Plans to expand mining operations in Kiruna, Sweden, threaten traditional grazing lands used by Sami reindeer herders. Photograph: Johan Ylitalo/The Guardian It coincides with rising anti-Sami rhetoric in Sweden, including from political leaders, amid clashes over land used for grazing by Sami reindeer herders for hundreds of years, which the state wants to mine for rare-earth minerals. The report says issues with the handling of Sami land rights in Sweden have been “reinforced and aggravated” by an ideology that Sami people are “an inferior people and therefore neither deserving of nor capable of exercising the same rights and responsibilities as other citizens”. It adds that the Swedish state has failed to implement the United Nations declaration on the rights of Indigenous peoples . The commission’s 71-point call to action recommends an official apology for the harm and injustice inflicted upon the Sami people, as well as financial compensation and completing the process of ratifying the International Labour Organization’s convention on Indigenous and tribal peoples . skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion It calls for the establishment of a national centre for redress and reconciliation, and for authorities to recognise that the Swedish nation was founded on lands belonging to two peoples – the Sámi and the Swedes – and that parts of the land have Sami names and are part of Sami cultural heritage. It also urges recognition that Sápmi, the region traditionally inhabited by the Sami people, extends across present national borders; an end to racial discrimination against Sami people; and better provision for children to learn Sami languages. It adds that the Swedish government must uphold the Sami people’s right to practise reindeer husbandry and other cultural practices on their traditional lands. The report concludes that the state, including the Swedish parliament, government and public authorities, and in some cases the Church of Sweden, must “bear responsibility” for policies and decisions that led to the violation of Sami rights. It says: “Accepting responsibility also requires the state to work towards providing redress for the harm inflicted on the Sami people and individual Sami, while pursuing policies that do not repeat these historical injustices.” Explore more on these topics Sweden Indigenous peoples Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
